Why spend our limited time on endless quarrels?

Karim Saab reflects on the brevity of life, the freedom of forgiveness, and the quiet strength of living with purpose.

Read the article

Full approved article

The world isn't paradise—but it is a precious opportunity

In the rush of everyday life, a small disagreement can suddenly feel like our entire world: an awkward word, a misunderstanding, or an old wound that refuses to fade. Then a quiet moment arrives, and we ask ourselves: does this really deserve so much of my peace?

Life is too short to spend it counting one another's mistakes, and too rich to be reduced to arguments. This world is not paradise; things will not always go our way. Yet every day offers us another chance to be calmer, kinder, and closer to what truly matters.

When the numbers put our lives in perspective

According to estimates published by the Population Reference Bureau, roughly 117 billion people had been born on Earth by 2022. Those alive at that time represented nearly seven percent of this estimated total. These are not exact counts; they are a scientific attempt to understand humanity's long journey.

Every one of those lives held dreams and hopes, families and friendships, joy and disappointment, and ordinary days much like ours. Their passing leaves us with a simple reminder: few things deserve our entire lifetime—least of all a feud with no end.

What will matter a century from now?

Imagine looking at the world a hundred years from now, in 2126. Faces, cities, and priorities will have changed, and many of today's urgent concerns will be distant memories. Two hundred years from now, in 2226, the present that feels so enormous to us may be just a small chapter in a much longer story.

This is not a reason to despair about passing time. It is a reason to value it. Each day can hold something worthwhile: strengthening a family bond, helping someone, speaking a healing word, or doing honest work with care.

We don't have to win every argument

How many friendships have drifted apart because of a misunderstanding? How many good days have been spoiled by our need to have the last word? Not every disagreement needs to become a permanent separation, and not every hurt must be carried for years.

Sometimes the greater victory is to let go—to keep our dignity without losing our humanity. We may disagree, and healthy boundaries may be necessary, but we do not have to live imprisoned by resentment.

The purpose that helps us find our way

When life feels crowded with distractions, I return to the Qur'anic reminder: 'I did not create jinn and humans except to worship Me' (Adh-Dhariyat 51:56). It reminds me that our lives have a purpose greater than rivalry or appearances.

Living with faith and kindness also means striving to fulfil our responsibilities, being of use to others, and keeping our hearts as clear as we can. We need not let the noise of small things drown out the direction of our lives.

Choose what deserves a place in your heart

Not every day will be easy, and we cannot always change people or circumstances. But, as much as we are able, we can choose how we respond and what receives our limited time.

Let us put down some of the weight of resentment, make room for forgiveness and peace, and fill our days with care and useful work. The world is not paradise, but it can become more beautiful when we leave behind kindness rather than conflict.

From the reflections and experiences of Abdulkarim bin Ibrahim Al Saab — KARIM SAAB
